quoted_passages: There is no certain plastic representation of the fravaši s.

Moulton accordingly (p. 260), rejecting the then prevailing Western interpretation of the Achaemenid winged symbol as that of Ahura Mazdā, identified it as the king's fravaši, and it is still generally regarded as a fravaši symbol by Zoroastrians.

Strong arguments, however, have by now been put forward by Western scholars for its representing xᵛarənah (for references see Boyce, Zoroastrianism II, p. 103 n. 82; Boyce and Grenet, Zoroastrianism III, p. 104 and nn. 197-98).
fresh_retrievals.passage_support_scope: Same published article as the round-6 main source, freshly re-fetched in round 8: the Ahuramazda reading of the Achaemenid winged symbol is characterized as 'the then prevailing Western interpretation' (i.e. a modern scholarly identification, not an ancient caption); Moulton's fravaši reading is recorded and remains a living Zoroastrian reading; the xᵛarənah reading is recorded as backed by 'strong arguments' from Western scholars. This is passage-level support for the coexistence of the three named identifications and for the fravaši reading's reception status.
fresh_retrievals.limits: Boyce 2000 scholarship consulted through a 2026 archive snapshot, not the print fascicle; the snapshot's byte count (400,626) differs by 2 bytes from the round-6 fetch (400,628) — replay wrapper variance, article text identical in the quoted sentences. The article does not settle any identification; it records the debate and the absence of a certain ancient fravaši representation.

fresh_retrievals.locator: Chapter 4 ('The Pantheon'), khvarenah discussion across pp. 299-300 (running heads '300 CHAPTER FOUR' and 'THE PANTHEON 301' bracket the quoted sentences); footnotes 65, 188-190. OCR line numbers: 17484-17551 (main passage), 5895-5901 (footnote 65).
quoted_passages: There has been a long debate on the concept of khvarenah in the Achaemenian royal ideology, and on its possible representation in Achaemenian art. The debate on the representation has focused on the well-known "figure in the winged disk," prominently represented in Achaemenian imperial art. Three interpretations have been offered for this figure: it was seen as the representation of the fravasi (guardian spirit) of the king, of Ahura Mazda himself, and of the royal khvarenah.

It is at present perhaps impossible to reach a consensus, but the argument advanced by A.Sh. Shahbazi and others, that the exact similitude between the figure in the winged disk and the king makes an interpretation of the figure as Ahura Mazda unlikely, appears to be very strong.

The suggestion that it represents khvarenah was argued most fully by A.Sh. Shahbazi, 'An Achaemenid symbol I. A farewell to "Fravahr and Ahuramazda"', AMI 7 (1974) 135-144; 'An Achaemenid symbol II. Farnah "(God given) Fortune" symbolised', AMI 13 (1980) 119-147. (footnote 189)

These theories are summed up in P. Lecoq, 'Un probleme de religion achemenide: Ahura Mazda ou Xvarnah?', in: Orientalia J. Duchesne-Guillemin Oblata (AI 23), Leiden 1984, 301-326, pp. 311-320. Lecoq defends an interpretation of the figure as Ahura Mazda. (footnote 189, continuation)

the figure in the winged disk — prominent in many pieces of Achaemenian art — represents a divine figure, be it Ahura Mazda (thus, among many others, P. Lecoq, …) or divine glory (thus, among many others, A.Sh. Shahbazi, 'An Achaemenid Symbol II: Farnah "(God given) Fortune" symbolised', AMI 13 (1980), 119-147). (footnote 65)

Shahbazi …' (in the raw stream the unrelated fragment 'Guests at a royal banquet' immediately precedes 'was argued most fully'). No wording was changed; raw fragments verified by grep at /tmp/r8-f12-scratch/magi.txt lines 17484-17555. The OCR also contains misreadings elsewhere (e.g. 'Grientalia', 'JTproastrianism'); the book's printed form was not inspected.
fresh_retrievals.passage_support_scope: Peer-reviewed monograph passage that (a) names exactly the three competing identifications — fravasi of the king, Ahura Mazda, royal khvarenah; (b) states consensus is 'perhaps impossible'; (c) records the Shahbazi argument as 'very strong' but does not declare it settled; (d) locates Shahbazi's own case bibliographically (fn. 189 to AMI 7, 1974 and AMI 13, 1980); (e) records that Lecoq (1984) defends the Ahuramazda reading. This is the strongest fresh secondary locator for the Shahbazi leg and for the entry's 'contested' calibration.
fresh_retrievals.limits: Shahbazi 1974 itself still not read directly (see access_limits_and_failures); de Jong's judgment is a secondary appraisal. OCR text, not the printed book; page numbers inferred from running heads. No ancient caption or object inspected.

quoted_passages: In the first article, An Achaemenid Symbol (Part) I, A Farewell to Fravahr and Ahuramazda, Shahbazi noted why he felt the farohar motif could not represent either the farohar/fravahar or Ahura Mazda. In his second article, An Achaemenid Symbol (Part) II, Farnah (God Given) Fortune Symbolised, Shahbazi fills the void with his dissertation on why the motif represented the khvarenah/farr which he calls 'farnah' by its Median-Achaemenid era (Old Persian) manifestation.
